summary: Honda's first electric car in Australia is a kei-car-based four-seat city hatch that Australian reviewers find genuinely fun, with a Boost mode that lifts output to 70 kW and adds simulated gearshifts, plus a generous standard specification. The catch is value and practicality: at $36,900 drive-away it costs well over the BYD Atto 1 and Geely EX2 while offering a 29.6 kWh battery, 202 km of WLTP range and a 162-litre boot. Supply is the other hurdle, with the first allocation of about 130 cars sold out within hours and waits of up to a year reported, and Honda has no plans to submit it for an ANCAP rating.
pros: Reviewers rate it a genuinely entertaining city car: Boost mode raises output from 47 kW to 70 kW and adds simulated gearshifts and engine sound
Honda's fixed national drive-away price ($36,900 Mono Tone, $37,400 Two Tone) means no dealer haggling and the same price in Melbourne as anywhere else
Light at about 1,093 kg, and efficient: 14.8 kWh/100km WLTP on 15-inch wheels
5-year unlimited-km warranty extends to up to 8 years via Honda Extend when serviced at Honda; battery covered for 8 years/160,000 km; five services capped at $199 each
cons: Dearer than direct rivals: the BYD Atto 1 starts at $23,990 before on-roads with a similar range, and the Atto 1 Premium and Geely EX2 Inspire offer 310-345 km WLTP for less
Short 202 km WLTP range from a 29.6 kWh battery (28 kWh usable), and DC charging tops out at 50 kW
Strict four-seater with a 162-litre boot (618 L to the window line with the rear seats folded)
Severely limited supply: about 130 cars for 2026 sold out before launch, with waits of up to 12 months depending on colour
No ANCAP rating, and Honda Australia says it has no plans to submit the car for testing
